item.title: Goshikidai Plateau: Scenic Heights over the Sea — Guide
item.description: Goshikidai is a broad lava plateau rising between Takamatsu and Sakaide on the Kagawa coast, its name (‘five-colour heights’) referring to five hills. A scenic road crosses the plateau, linking viewpoints, walking trails, a planetarium and quiet woodland, with sweeping panoramas over the Seto Inland Sea and its islands. From its western edge there are especially fine views of the great Seto Ohashi bridge striding across the water toward Honshu, magnificent at sunset and when lit at night.

item.title: Washuzan Hill: The Seto Ohashi Bridge Viewpoint — Guide
item.description: Washuzan is a modest hill of just 133 metres on the southern coast of Kurashiki, but its view is one of the finest in western Japan. From its granite outcrops the whole eastern Seto Inland Sea opens out below: dozens of green islands scattered across the water, ships threading between them, and the vast Seto Ohashi bridge striding across the strait to Shikoku on a series of enormous suspension spans. It is celebrated as one of Japan’s great sunset spots, when the sea turns gold and the bridge is silhouetted, and later the bridge itself is illuminated.

item.title: Yashima: Flat-Topped Plateau and History — Guide
item.description: Yashima is a striking flat-topped lava plateau that rises steeply above the coast just east of Takamatsu, its level summit and sheer sides making it a local landmark. From the top, terraces and viewpoints command sweeping panoramas over Takamatsu, the island-dotted Seto Inland Sea, and the surrounding coast — especially beautiful at sunset. The plateau is steeped in history: it was the site of the Battle of Yashima in 1185, a famous clash of the Genpei War between the Minamoto and Taira clans, remembered in legend and place names.

item.title: Cape Hedo Guide: Okinawa's Northern Tip, Cliffs & Access
item.description: Cape Hedo (Hedo Misaki) is the wild northernmost point of Okinawa’s main island, where rugged limestone cliffs meet the deep blue of the open sea. A windswept viewpoint with crashing waves below, it offers sweeping panoramas and, on clear days, a glimpse of distant Yoron and Okinoerabu islands to the north. The cape also carries historical weight: a monument here commemorates Okinawa’s 1972 reversion to Japan. Paired with the karst formations of nearby Daisekirinzan and the Yanbaru forest, it’s the grand finale of a northern road trip.
